schools.summary: Gill dates the turn of the year by the Targum, the month Adar closing it.
Henry credits David with following his blow and then makes the tarrying at Jerusalem the hinge of the chapter.
Clarke sets the season by Calmet’s two campaigns; Wesley explains the going forth of kings from the state of the ground.
Ellicott reconstructs the division of forces, notes the written Hebrew reads “when angels go forth”, and reads the destruction as the wasting of the country.

debates.question: Why is spring the season for the campaign?

sides.position: The ground is then fit for the march of soldiers and brings forth provision for man and beast
It is the most proper season for military operations, winter being inconvenient and summer too hot
Because the previous campaign closed with the rainy season spent at Jerusalem

outliers.note: He notes that by the insertion of a letter the written Hebrew reads not “when kings go forth” but “when angels, or messengers, go forth”, corrected in the margin.

themes: at the return of the year
when kings go forth to battle
1.pericope_label: In the time when kings go forth, David tarried at Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill fixes the hour by the sightline, the sun declining but not yet dusk.
Ellicott works out what the palace roof overlooked and lays the fall to uninterrupted prosperity; Keil and Delitzsch call it a turning-point and blame the tolerated polygamy.
Henry supplies the phrase about the bed of sloth that Wesley repeats.
Clarke argues both sides of Bathsheba’s blame; Wesley puts her in a garden bath cleansing from ceremonial pollution.

debates.question: Was the woman at fault for being seen?

sides.position: The suspicion presses hard: no woman of delicacy would expose herself in view of the king’s terrace
Yet in Bengal women bathe in open pools morning and evening, so David might have seen her with no blame attaching
The court was probably concealed from every point but the palace roof, from which no harm was suspected

debates.question: What accounts for David’s fall at this point?

sides.position: Long uninterrupted prosperity and power, which had intoxicated him and thrown him off his guard
The tolerated polygamy that encouraged licentiousness, barely checked by the warning to kings
Idleness: the bed of sloth often proves the bed of lust

outliers.note: He passes on a word of Augustine’s, that David’s fall should put upon their guard those who have not fallen and save from despair those who have.

themes: the siesta and the palace roof
2.pericope_label: David sees the woman washing from the roof

schools.summary: Gill allows the enquiry may have been innocent at first and still judges it better never made.
Keil and Delitzsch weigh the spellings in Samuel against those in Chronicles and decline to rule on the father’s name; Ellicott marks Uriah’s place among the thirty.
Henry reads David’s intention as genuinely open at that moment.
Clarke hears the terms of the covenant in the name Eliam itself.

debates.question: Was the enquiry itself culpable?

sides.position: Perhaps not at first: he may have meant marriage if she were single, and nothing dishonourable
It was: instead of suppressing the desire the sight had kindled, he sought to feed it
Better never to have inquired at all, but to have stifled the motions raised at the sight of her

debates.question: Which form of the names is original?

sides.position: Bathsheba is correct and original, on the evidence of the succession narrative
Of Eliam and Ammiel, which came first is impossible to determine
Such inversion is a frequent variation among Scripture names, and both render God’s people and the people of God

outliers.note: He hears the covenant formula in the name — I will be your God, we will be thy people — rendering the pair as the people of my God and the God of my people.

themes: the wife of Uriah the Hittite
3.pericope_label: Enquiry after the woman: Bathsheba, wife of Uriah

schools.summary: Gill records only that the messengers went to invite her to the palace.
Keil and Delitzsch deny craft or violence and hold Bathsheba not free from blame; Ellicott corrects the tense of the clause about her purifying and reads the law behind it.
Clarke makes the washing a point of physiology and the conception its proof; Wesley draws the downhill slope of sin.

debates.question: Was Bathsheba taken by force?

sides.position: No: there is no intimation of craft or violence, and she came at his request without hesitation
The words do not imply violence; she yielded without resistance, perhaps flattered by the king’s approach
We hear nothing of her reluctance and there is no evidence of force
Not by force, but by persuasion

debates.question: What is the clause about her purifying for?

sides.position: A point of law: read “and she was”, she being unclean until evening, so she stayed in the palace till then
A point of physiology: it marks the time at which conception is most likely, which the conceiving proves

outliers.note: He observes that she was scrupulous in the detail of her uncleanness while conscious of a capital crime, and adds that David was nevertheless a far greater offender.

themes: he sent messengers and took her
not by force but by persuasion
she was purified from her uncleanness
4.pericope_label: David takes her, and the message: I am with child

schools.summary: Gill measures the distance to Rabbah on Bunting’s authority, sixty-four miles.
Keil and Delitzsch fix Uriah’s rank among the gibborim and reject Josephus on his office; Ellicott sets out the three steps of the plan.
Henry works out the two dangers the summons was meant to avert and reads the pretext as transparent.

debates.question: What post did Uriah hold?

sides.position: One of the gibborim, and therefore some post of command
Not Joab’s armour-bearer or aide-de-camp, for which Josephus has no historical foundation

debates.question: What was David trying to prevent?

sides.position: A prosecution of the wife under the law, jealousy being the rage of a man of honour
A rebellion, there being no legal remedy against a king, and kings have lost crowns over such provocations
Simply the discovery of the crime, by having the child supposed Uriah’s own

outliers.note: He judges it likely that Bathsheba would never have consented without a promise of protection beforehand, and adds that hope of impunity is a great encouragement to iniquity.

themes: fathering the child upon the husband
the pretext of a report from the war

schools.summary: Gill has Uriah report to the palace before his own house and reconstructs his evening among the guards.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the custom of washing the feet after a journey; Ellicott renders the dish literally as a present and denies Uriah suspected anything.
Henry reports both views of Uriah’s motive and settles it from the unopened letter.
Clarke calls the whole arrangement artfully contrived and marks the limit of David’s design at this stage; Wesley makes the staying away a work of providence.

debates.question: Did Uriah stay away because he suspected?

sides.position: His suspicions had been aroused, the connection perhaps not having remained a secret
It is quite unnecessary to suppose any suspicion; his conduct is simply that of a frank, generous soldier
Had he suspected, he would surely have opened the letter he afterwards carried to Joab
Providence put the resolution into his heart, to bring David’s sin to light

outliers.note: He marks the limit of the design at this stage: David as yet had no intention of murdering Uriah, nor of taking Bathsheba to wife.

themes: go down to thy house and wash thy feet
a mess of meat from the king
he slept at the door of the king’s house
7.pericope_label: Go down to thy house; but Uriah slept at the door

schools.summary: Gill records the refusal as Uriah’s apology for his conduct.

Keil and Delitzsch gloss the huts as equivalent to the open field and reconstruct the argument; Ellicott grants the custom of carrying the ark and denies the mention of Israel and Judah dates the book late.
Henry alone leaves open whether the ark went to the camp, and sets the refusal against the law it exceeds.
Clarke takes the words at face value and calls it the answer of a brave and disinterested man; Wesley draws the rule about abstaining from lawful delights.

debates.question: Had the ark actually gone out with the army?

sides.position: Yes: it appears they had taken it with them to battle
Yes, and the practice was usual, for the army’s encouragement and direction
The custom persisted despite its capture in the days of Eli
It was in a tent either way, at home or in the camp, and which is not certain

outliers.note: He sets the refusal beside the statute requiring a man on campaign to keep himself from every wicked thing, and draws the comparison: Uriah outdid that law, and David violated it.

themes: the ark and Israel abide in tents
shall I go into mine house?
as thou livest, I will not do this thing
10.pericope_label: The ark and the tents: Uriah refuses to go down

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the hope behind the supper; Ellicott declines to comment on the attempt and marks what it proved of Uriah’s resolve.
Henry refuses to treat the act as a stratagem merely.
Clarke explains the calculation, that off his guard he would hasten home.

outliers.note: He makes the drunkenness a sin in itself whatever its design, holding that robbing a man of his reason is worse than robbing him of his money.

themes: he did eat and drink before him
he went not down to his house
12.pericope_label: Tarry here today also, and the supper that made him drunk

schools.summary: Gill ascribes the new method to Satan’s suggestion once the first plan failed.
Keil and Delitzsch measure the fall against David’s earlier scruples; Ellicott notes the double use made of the man and Joab’s unquestioning obedience.
Henry counts the aggravations and compares the method with Absalom’s and Ahab’s.
Clarke calls it the sum of treachery and fetches the Bellerophon parallel only to reject it.

debates.question: Is the Bellerophon story a parallel to Uriah’s?

sides.position: Many have thought it not merely parallel but a fabulous formation out of this history
There is scarcely any correspondence beyond the single circumstance that both carried letters containing their own condemnation

outliers.note: He finds a paradox in the sending: David could bear such malice toward the one man he still trusted with sealed orders he must not read.

themes: David wrote a letter to Joab
sent by the hand of Uriah
14.pericope_label: The letter sent by the hand of Uriah

schools.summary: Gill records the verse as the orders given to Joab, without gloss.
Keil and Delitzsch render both clauses closely; Ellicott observes that only the first was obeyed and counts the cost of the disobedience.
Wesley turns from the letter to the writer, who seeks to cover one sin with another.

debates.question: Did Joab understand what he was being asked to do?

sides.position: The literal fulfilment does not warrant assuming he suspected, or had heard any rumour
He anticipated the king’s pleasure in the death, which he connected with his own losses

outliers.note: He notes that the order to retire was not carried out, perhaps because it would make the stratagem too evident or was impracticable, so that others died with Uriah and the guilt grew beyond the letter.

themes: set ye Uriah in the forefront
15.pericope_label: Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle

schools.summary: Gill reads the survey as reconnaissance of the city’s strongest point and reports the Targum’s “besieged”.
Ellicott renders the verb as watched or blockaded and makes the disposition deliberate; Keil and Delitzsch place the brave men inside the city and explain Joab’s faithfulness as self-interest.
Clarke has Joab and his men retire from Uriah in the heat of the assault.

debates.question: Was the order to withdraw from Uriah carried out?

sides.position: Yes: in the heat of the assault Joab and his men retired from him
No: that part of the orders was never carried out, which is why others fell with him

debates.question: Whose valour does “valiant men” describe?

sides.position: The defenders inside the city, which is what made the position deadly

outliers.note: They explain Joab’s faithfulness in this point not by loyalty but by exchange, so that his own interests might be served another time.

themes: a place where valiant men were
16.pericope_label: Joab assigns the place, and Uriah dies

schools.summary: Gill reads the instruction as stagecraft, to be used according to the king’s countenance.
Keil and Delitzsch give the conditional in full and identify Jerubbosheth as Gideon; Ellicott holds the messenger could not have seen through the errand.
Henry holds that the instruction gave too broad an intimation, and praises the soldiers’ familiarity with their bibles.
Clarke supplies a motive of self-protection: Joab had losses of his own to explain away.

debates.question: Could the messenger see through his errand?

sides.position: No: it would appear rather as an effort to shift blame onto Uriah as leader of the assault
Yes: it gave too broad an intimation to him, and through him to others, for murder will out

debates.question: Why did Joab prepare for the king’s anger at all?

sides.position: He expected displeasure at the losses from approaching imprudently close to the wall
He had suffered loss by some indiscretion of his own and contrived to connect it with a welcome death

outliers.note: He takes the citation of Abimelech as evidence that the book of Judges was already published in Samuel’s time and that even the soldiers could quote the scripture story as a warning.

themes: thy servant Uriah is dead also
18.pericope_label: Joab charges the messenger, and remembers Abimelech

schools.summary: Gill supplies the hardware of the shooting and explains how the range was closed.
Keil and Delitzsch note the messenger condensed his report and describe David’s apparent composure; Ellicott hears a special regret for Uriah in the wording.
Henry hears secret satisfaction and catches the contradiction in the order to press the siege.
Clarke calls the reply abominable hypocrisy outright.

debates.question: What does David’s reply amount to?

sides.position: Apparent composure on news he was anxious to hear, and a refusal to call the affair disastrous
Encouragement, yet couched so as to imply a special regret for the loss of so brave a man
Abominable hypocrisy: he knew the death was no chance-medley
Secret satisfaction: all is well now that Uriah is out of the way

outliers.note: He catches the contradiction in the last clause: David orders the battle made stronger against the city while his own sin was weakening it and provoking God to blast the undertaking.

themes: the shooters shot from off the wall
the sword devoureth one as well as another
23.pericope_label: The report delivered, and David's answer to Joab

schools.summary: Gill explains how she heard, and why David wanted the death published quickly.
Ellicott cites the seven-day precedents and judges the term shortened as far as decency allowed; Keil and Delitzsch pass the verse without comment.
Henry reads the mourning as a ceremony submitted to for the shortest time custom would admit.
Clarke judges the form observed without the power of sorrow.

debates.question: Was the mourning genuine?

sides.position: No: the whole of her conduct shows the form observed without the feeling — she lost a captain and got a king
However long it ran, it was made as short as was consistent with decency
It was a ceremony submitted to for as short a time as custom would admit

outliers.note: He suggests David wanted the death published abroad as quickly as possible, the more effectually to hide his own sin, while thinking it probable the widow knew nothing of the plot.

themes: the form without the power of sorrow
published abroad to hide a sin
26.pericope_label: The wife of Uriah mourned for her husband

schools.summary: Gill measures the haste against the later ninety-day rule and reports Abarbinel’s charge.
Henry gathers the adultery, falsehood, murder and marriage under the one divine verdict.
Clarke turns the chapter into an argument for the honesty of Scripture and apportions blame in four verdicts; Wesley reads the months of impenitence as an instance of the deceitfulness of sin.
Ellicott asks why David was left so long unconvicted and refuses to read the silence as a quiet conscience.

debates.question: Why was David left so long without conviction?

sides.position: So that the sin might be fastened on him openly, beyond denial, by the birth of the child
His conscience was at work meantime, preparing him for the prophet’s visit
It is an instance of the judgment of God in punishing one sin by delivering a man up to another

debates.question: How is the blame to be apportioned?

sides.position: Four verdicts: pity for David, veneration for Uriah, detestation for Joab, contempt for Bathsheba
Bathsheba was probably first in the transgression
The whole matter was displeasing to the LORD, who hates sin most in those nearest him in profession

outliers.note: He makes the chapter an illustrious proof of the truth of the sacred writings: no one inventing a religion would have inserted such an account of one of its brightest ornaments.

27.pericope_label: He took her to be his wife, and the thing displeased the LORD
